title: Consensus Mechanisms & Mining
intro: The PYRAX TriStream Consensus is the engine that keeps the network honest. Every block produced and every transaction confirmed flows through this mechanism. As a DevNet tester, you are observing and stress-testing this engine — which means you need to understand how it works, what can go wrong, and what you are responsible for.

sections.title: How Consensus Works
sections.content:
THE TRISTREAM MODEL
PYRAX runs three independent consensus streams simultaneously. Each stream is responsible for a different security property, and all three must agree for a block to reach finality:

Stream A (ASIC Mining): Produces block proposals using BLAKE3 and SHA-256 proof of work. Provides raw computational security — making it expensive to produce fraudulent blocks.
Stream B (CPU/GPU Mining): Produces competing block proposals using KAWPOW and RandomX. Ensures the network remains accessible to commodity hardware. GPU nodes can also opt into the AI Processing Pool.
Stream C (PoS Validation): Validators with staked PYRX vote on which block proposals from Streams A and B are valid. A supermajority (67%+) of staked weight must agree before finality.

FINALITY AND BLOCK TIMES
FINALITY: Once a block receives a supermajority PoS vote, it is final. It cannot be reversed, orphaned, or reorganised. This is a hard guarantee.
BLOCK TIME: Layer 1 targets approximately 60 seconds per block. Layer 3 ZK Rollup settlements happen much faster — multiple L3 batches can settle within a single L1 block.
FORKS: Because Stream A and Stream B produce competing proposals, temporary forks can occur. Stream C validators resolve these by voting on the canonical chain tip.

THE BLOCKCHAIN TRILEMMA
PYRAX's design choices address all three corners:
Security: TriStream requires an attacker to compromise PoW and PoS simultaneously — far more expensive than attacking either alone.
Decentralisation: CPU/GPU mining (Stream B) prevents ASIC dominance. PoS (Stream C) distributes finality across token holders.
Scalability: L3 ZK Rollups batch thousands of transactions and settle proofs on L1, achieving 500,000+ TPS without bloating the base layer.

sections.title: Mining Rules & Your Responsibilities
sections.content:
WHAT DEVNET TESTERS OBSERVE
During DevNet, you are not mining or staking on mainnet. However, you will observe and report on:
Block Production Rate: Is the L1 hitting its ~60s target? Report significant deviations.
Fork Events: The node logs indicate temporary forks with a FORK keyword. These are expected occasionally — but if forks do not resolve within 3–5 blocks, that is a reportable anomaly.
Consensus Failures: If your node loses consensus with the majority and gets stuck on a minority chain, that is a high-severity incident.

PROTOCOL RULES YOU MUST FOLLOW
All DevNet testers running nodes must adhere to the following:
No Consensus Interference: Do not attempt to manipulate block proposals, replay transactions, or intentionally cause forks. This is a critical violation.
Proper Staking Configuration (if staking): Your stake must remain above the minimum threshold (1,000 PYRX on DevNet). Dropping below without notice invalidates your node's votes.
Slashing Conditions: Validators who double-sign (vote for two competing blocks at the same height) are slashed. On DevNet, slashing removes accrued PYRX rewards, not real tokens.
Upgrade Compliance: If a consensus rule change is released (a hard fork), all validators must upgrade within 72 hours or their votes are rejected by upgraded peers.

REPORTING CONSENSUS ANOMALIES
If you observe any of the following, file a High or Critical incident report immediately:
Fork that does not resolve within 5 blocks
Consensus halt (no new blocks for 10+ minutes)
Node stuck on minority chain (your head is behind the majority by 20+ blocks)
Double-sign accusation in logs (SLASHING_DETECTED keyword)

quiz.question: A PYRAX block reaches 'finality' when which condition is met?
options: When Stream A (ASIC miners) produce the block with the most accumulated proof-of-work
When a supermajority (67%+) of staked PYRX in Stream C votes to confirm the block
When the block has been in the chain for more than 6 subsequent blocks
When both Stream A and Stream B produce identical block proposals
quiz.explanation: Finality in PYRAX requires a supermajority PoS vote from Stream C validators — specifically 67%+ of staked weight. Once reached, the block is irreversible. It is not based on accumulated PoW depth (like Bitcoin's 6-block rule) or on matching proposals between streams.

quiz.question: A tester notices in their node logs that a fork has occurred. After how many unresolved blocks should they file a high-severity incident report?
options: Immediately — any fork is a critical incident requiring an instant report
After 1 block — forks should never occur on a healthy network
After 3 to 5 blocks — if the fork has not resolved by then, it is a reportable anomaly
After 20 blocks — the network always self-resolves within that window
quiz.explanation: Temporary forks are a normal part of TriStream consensus since Streams A and B produce competing proposals simultaneously. Stream C resolves these by voting on the canonical tip. A fork not resolved within 3–5 blocks is anomalous and should be reported as a high-severity incident.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of Stream B (CPU/GPU Mining) in the TriStream model?
options: To provide computational security by making fraudulent blocks expensive to produce
To aggregate PoS votes from validators and enforce finality
To ensure the network remains accessible to commodity hardware and prevent ASIC dominance
To batch Layer 3 transactions and settle ZK proofs on Layer 1
quiz.explanation: Stream B (KAWPOW and RandomX) is specifically designed to keep block production accessible to CPU and GPU miners, preventing ASICs from monopolising the network. Stream A provides the PoW computational security. Stream C handles PoS finality. ZK Rollup settlement is a Layer 3 function.

quiz.question: A DevNet tester running a PoS validator node intentionally double-signs to test how the network reacts. What is the consequence?
options: Nothing — double-signing is allowed during DevNet for testing purposes
The node is temporarily disconnected from peers but reconnects automatically
The validator's accrued DevNet PYRX rewards are slashed
The validator is issued a warning but keeps all rewards
quiz.explanation: Double-signing (voting for two competing blocks at the same height) is a slashable offence. On DevNet, this results in slashing of accrued PYRX rewards. It is NOT a permitted test action — intentional consensus interference is a critical protocol violation that can result in removal from the programme.

quiz.question: A hard fork (consensus rule change) is released. A validator fails to upgrade within the required window. What happens to their votes?
options: Their votes are still counted — the network is backwards-compatible
Their votes are rejected by upgraded peers, effectively removing them from the active validator set
They are automatically upgraded by the network without any action required
Their stake is returned and they must re-register as a validator
quiz.explanation: After a hard fork, all upgraded peers enforce the new consensus rules. Votes from non-upgraded validators do not conform to the new rules and are therefore rejected. This effectively removes them from the active validator set until they upgrade. Upgrade compliance is mandatory within 72 hours of a release.
